<div role="note" aria-label="Note" class="callout-note" markdown="1">
**Update (25 November 2026)**

The maps now use **ggplot2**, with a final comparison of the five grid methods
alongside the original boundaries.
</div>

Sometimes you want to produce maps with special layouts. I especially like maps
with modified geometries, e.g. simplifying the original shapes to squares or
dots. When searching the web, I found the fantastic post [Fishnets and
Honeycomb: Square vs. Hexagonal Spatial
Grids](https://strimas.com/post/hexagonal-grids/) by [Matt
Strimas-Mackey](https://strimas.com/#about), which was a huge inspiration (by
the way, don't miss [his blog](http://strimas.com/#posts), full of very
interesting pieces of work).

The only thing I was not completely comfortable with was that the post used the
[old-fashioned](https://r.geocompx.org/) **sp** package instead of my personal
favorite, the **sf** package. The post was published in 2016, and note that the
author has also moved to the **sf** package since then. So I decided to explore
further options with **sf**.

The approach is similar, using grids over a map and working with them, but with
[`st_make_grid()`](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/reference/st_make_grid.html).
I also expanded it by grouping the grids and producing dots over the geometries.
So basically I produced five variations of the map:

| Type          | Replacement | Grouped |
|---------------|:-----------:|:-------:|
| **Fishnet**   |   Square    |   No    |
| **Puzzle**    |   Square    |   Yes   |
| **Honeycomb** |   Hexagon   |   No    |
| **Hexbin**    |   Hexagon   |   Yes   |
| **Pixel**     |     Dot     |   No    |


<div role="note" aria-label="Tip" class="callout-tip" markdown="1">

This technique works best with less detailed, simplified geometries.

</div>

## Required **R** packages

```{r}
#| label: libs

library(sf)
library(giscoR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)

# Define a common theme for the maps.
background <- "#FAF8F2"
foreground <- "#203B47"

map_title <- "inter-tight"
map_regular <- "inter"

sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_title)
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter", family = map_regular)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()

sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_title)
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter", family = map_regular)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()

theme_set(
  theme_grey(paper = background, base_family = map_regular, ink = foreground) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold"),
      legend.title = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold"),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = background),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = background),
      strip.text = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold"),
      strip.clip = "off",
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
)
```

## Working with square grids

Let's use the `square` option of `st_make_grid()` and play a bit with it.

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_preparing
#| fig-cap: ""
uk <- gisco_get_nuts(
  year = 2021, country = "GBR", nuts_level = 1, epsg = 3857,
  resolution = 20
) %>%
  # # Group by nation
  mutate(NAME_EN = case_when(
    str_detect(NUTS_NAME, "Wales|Scotland|Ireland") ~ NUTS_NAME,
    TRUE ~ "England"
  )) %>%
  group_by(NAME_EN) |>
  summarise(do_union = TRUE) %>%
  # Iteration using indexes
  mutate(index_target = row_number())

uk_palette <- c(
  England = "#A33C45",
  Scotland = "#345F91",
  Wales = "#477C54",
  "Northern Ireland" = "#A7A6D5"
)
```

<div role="note" aria-label="Caution" class="callout-caution" markdown="1">
The `cellsize` should be set in the same unit as the projection (in this case,
meters). Smaller cells create denser grids and can use substantially more memory.
</div>

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_squares
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Two maps of the United Kingdom comparing separate square cells with cells
#|   merged into regional shapes. Colors distinguish regions.

# Grid to sf
grid <- uk %>%
  st_make_grid(50 * 1000,
    # Kms
    crs = st_crs(uk),
    what = "polygons",
    square = TRUE
  ) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  mutate(index = row_number())

# We identify the grids that belong to an entity by assessing the centroid
cent_merge <- grid %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  st_filter(uk) %>%
  st_join(uk)

grid_new <- grid %>% inner_join(st_drop_geometry(cent_merge), by = "index")

# Fishnet
fish_geom <- grid_new %>%
  group_by(NAME_EN) %>%
  summarise(do_union = FALSE)


# Now let's create the puzzle
puzzle_geom <- grid_new %>%
  # Avoid slivers
  st_buffer(0.5) %>%
  group_by(NAME_EN) %>%
  summarise(do_union = TRUE) # The only difference is do_union

# Plot

fish_geom %>%
  mutate(label = "Fishnet") %>%
  bind_rows(
    puzzle_geom %>%
      mutate(label = "Puzzle")
  ) %>%
  mutate(label = forcats::fct_inorder(label)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = NAME_EN),
    colour = background,
    linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~label) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = uk_palette) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = rel(1.2), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
      margin = margin(b = 10)
    )
  )
```

## Going hex

Extremely easy. We just need to change the `square` parameter of
`st_make_grid()` from `TRUE` to `FALSE`.

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_hex
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Two maps of the United Kingdom comparing separate hexagonal cells with
#|   cells merged into regional shapes. Colors distinguish regions.

# Grid to sf
grid_hex <- uk %>%
  st_make_grid(50 * 1000,
    # Kms
    crs = st_crs(uk),
    what = "polygons",
    square = FALSE # This is the only piece that changes!!!
  ) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  mutate(index = row_number())

cent_merge_hex <- grid_hex %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  st_filter(uk) %>%
  st_join(uk)

grid_hex_new <- grid_hex %>%
  inner_join(st_drop_geometry(cent_merge_hex), by = "index")

# Honeycomb
honey_geom <- grid_hex_new %>%
  group_by(NAME_EN) %>%
  summarise(do_union = FALSE)


# Now let's create the hexbin
hexbin_geom <- grid_hex_new %>%
  # Avoid slivers
  st_buffer(0.5) %>%
  group_by(NAME_EN) %>%
  summarise(do_union = TRUE) # The only difference is do_union

# Plot

honey_geom %>%
  mutate(label = "Honeycomb") %>%
  bind_rows(
    hexbin_geom %>%
      mutate(label = "Hexbin")
  ) %>%
  mutate(label = forcats::fct_inorder(label)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = NAME_EN),
    colour = background,
    linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~label) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = uk_palette) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = rel(1.2), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
      margin = margin(b = 10)
    )
  )
```

## Pixel it!

For the dot map, use the centers of a hexagonal grid. Assign each center to a
region, then draw a circle with a radius set to 40% of the grid cell size.

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_pix
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Map of the United Kingdom made of round dots, with color distinguishing
#|   the four constituent countries.

grid_pixels <- uk %>%
  st_make_grid(50 * 1000,
    # Kms
    crs = st_crs(uk),
    what = "centers",
    square = FALSE
  ) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  mutate(index = row_number())

pixels_geom <- grid_pixels %>%
  st_join(uk, left = FALSE) %>%
  # We need to buffer the points to get polygons, based on the grid resolution
  st_buffer(50 * 1000 * 0.4) %>%
  group_by(NAME_EN) %>%
  summarise(do_union = FALSE)


# Plot
ggplot(pixels_geom) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = NAME_EN),
    colour = background,
    linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = uk_palette) +
  labs(title = "Pixel")
```

## Wrap up

Finally, I wrapped all that in [`stdh_gridpol()`](https://github.com/dieghernan/dieghernan.github.io/blob/main/assets/functions/stdh_gridpol.R).

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_function
stdh_gridpol <- function(sf,
                         to = "fishnet",
                         gridsize = as.integer(
                           min(
                             diff(st_bbox(sf)[c(1, 3)]),
                             diff(st_bbox(sf)[c(2, 4)])
                           ) / 40
                         ),
                         sliver = 0.5) {
  if (!all(st_geometry_type(sf) %in% c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON"))) {
    stop("Input should be MULTIPOLYGON or POLYGON")
  }
  if (!to %in% c("fishnet", "puzzle", "honeycomb", "hexbin", "pixel")) {
    stop("'to' should be 'fishnet','puzzle','honeycomb','hexbin' or 'pixel'")
  }

  if (inherits(sf, "sf")) {
    initial <- sf
    initial$index_target <- 1:nrow(initial)
  } else {
    initial <- st_sf(index_target = 1:length(sf), geom = sf)
  }

  target <- st_geometry(initial)

  if (to %in% c("fishnet", "puzzle")) {
    sq <- T
  } else {
    sq <- F
  }
  if (to == "pixel") {
    grid <- st_make_grid(target,
      gridsize,
      crs = st_crs(initial),
      what = "centers",
      square = FALSE
    )
  } else {
    grid <- st_make_grid(
      target,
      gridsize,
      crs = st_crs(initial),
      what = "polygons",
      square = sq
    )
  }
  grid <- st_sf(index = 1:length(lengths(grid)), grid) # Add index
  if (to == "pixel") {
    cent_merge <- st_join(grid, initial["index_target"], left = F)
    grid_new <- st_buffer(cent_merge, gridsize * 0.4)
  } else {
    cent_grid <- st_centroid(grid)
    cent_merge <- st_join(cent_grid, initial["index_target"], left = F)
    grid_new <- inner_join(grid, st_drop_geometry(cent_merge), by = "index")
  }
  if (to %in% c("fishnet", "honeycomb", "pixel")) {
    geom <- aggregate(
      grid_new,
      by = list(grid_new$index_target),
      FUN = min,
      do_union = FALSE
    )
  } else {
    geom <- aggregate(
      st_buffer(grid_new, sliver),
      by = list(grid_new$index_target),
      FUN = min,
      do_union = TRUE
    )
  }
  if (inherits(sf, "sf")) {
    fin <- left_join(
      geom %>% select(index_target),
      st_drop_geometry(initial),
      by = "index_target"
    ) %>%
      select(-index_target)
    fin <- st_cast(fin, "MULTIPOLYGON")
    return(fin)
  } else {
    fin <- st_cast(geom, "MULTIPOLYGON")
    return(st_geometry(fin))
  }
}
# End of the function-----

fish <- stdh_gridpol(uk, to = "fishnet", gridsize = 50 * 1000)
puzz <- stdh_gridpol(uk, to = "puzzle", gridsize = 50 * 1000)
hon <- stdh_gridpol(uk, to = "honeycomb", gridsize = 50 * 1000)
hex <- stdh_gridpol(uk, to = "hexbin", gridsize = 50 * 1000)
pix <- stdh_gridpol(uk, to = "pixel", gridsize = 50 * 1000)
```

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_functionex
#| fig-crop: true
#| fig-height: 7.75
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Six maps of the United Kingdom compare the original boundaries with square
#|   cells, merged squares, hexagonal cells, merged hexagons and dots.

grid_maps <- bind_rows(
  list(
    Map = uk,
    Fishnet = fish,
    Puzzle = puzz,
    Honeycomb = hon,
    Hexbin = hex,
    Pixel = pix
  ),
  .id = "method"
) |>
  mutate(
    method = factor(
      method,
      levels = c("Map", "Fishnet", "Puzzle", "Honeycomb", "Hexbin", "Pixel")
    )
  )

ggplot(grid_maps) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = NAME_EN),
    colour = background,
    linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = uk_palette) +
  facet_wrap(vars(method), nrow = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Redrawing the United Kingdom",
    subtitle = "Original boundaries and five representations on a 50 km grid"
  )
```

And that's it! The function `stdh_gridpol()` has some alert mechanisms, such as
accepting only `POLYGON` or `MULTIPOLYGON`, and the default value of `gridsize`
is computed so that the shortest dimension has 40 cells.

```{r}
#| label: 20190602_imgpost
#| include: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-height: 5.3
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-alt: "World map made of cyan dots on a dark gray background."
world <- gisco_get_coastal_lines() %>%
  st_transform("+proj=robin")
world2 <- stdh_gridpol(world, "pixel", gridsize = 300000)


ggplot(world2) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#1fc2ff", colour = "#505050", linewidth = 0.15) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#505050"),
    plot.margin = margin(1, 1, 1, 1)
  )
```
